paragraphs: Where was he running? “Where else could she be but at Fyodor Pavlovitch’s? She must have gone straight to him from Samsonov’s. That was clear now. The whole intrigue, the whole deceit, was plain.” ... It all went whirling through his mind. He did not run to Marya Kondratyevna’s. “No need to go there ... not the slightest need ... he must not raise an alarm ... they would run and tell right away.... Marya Kondratyevna was clearly in the plot, and Smerdyakov too, he too, all of them had been bought!”

He made another plan. He took a long way round Fyodor Pavlovitch’s house, crossing the lane, going down Dmitrovsky Street and over the little bridge. That brought him straight to the deserted alley at the back, which was empty and had no houses on it. On one side was the wattle fence of a neighbor’s kitchen-garden. On the other was the strong, high fence that ran all around Fyodor Pavlovitch’s garden. Here he picked a spot, apparently the very place where, according to the story he knew, Lizaveta had once climbed over. “If she could climb over it,” the thought came to him, God knows why, “surely I can.” He did in fact jump up, and at once managed to catch hold of the top of the fence. Then he pulled himself up with all his strength and sat astride it. Close by in the garden stood the bath-house, but from the fence he could also see the lighted windows of the house.

“Yes, the old man’s bedroom is lit up. She’s there!” And he leapt from the fence into the garden. He knew Grigory was ill, and very likely Smerdyakov too, and that there was no one to hear him. Still, he instinctively hid, stood motionless, and began to listen. But there was dead silence on all sides, and, as if on purpose, complete stillness, not the slightest breath of wind.

“And naught but the whispering silence,” the line came into his mind for some reason. “If only no one heard me jump over the fence! I don’t think they did.” He stood still for a minute, then walked softly over the grass in the garden, keeping clear of the trees and shrubs. He walked slowly, creeping stealthily at every step and listening to his own footsteps. It took him five minutes to reach the lighted window. He remembered that right under the window there were several thick, tall bushes of elder and whitebeam. The door from the house into the garden, on the left-hand side, was shut. He had looked carefully on purpose to see that, as he passed. At last he reached the bushes and hid behind them. He held his breath. “I must wait now,” he thought, “to calm them down, in case they heard my footsteps and are listening ... if only I don’t cough or sneeze.”

He waited two minutes. His heart was beating violently, and at moments he could hardly breathe. “No, this pounding in my heart won’t stop,” he thought. “I can’t wait any longer.” He was standing behind a bush in the shadow. The light from the window fell on the front of the bush.

“How red the whitebeam berries are!” he murmured, not knowing why. Softly and noiselessly, step by step, he approached the window and raised himself on tiptoe. Fyodor Pavlovitch’s whole bedroom lay open before him. It was not a large room. A red screen divided it in two, “Chinese,” as Fyodor Pavlovitch used to call it. The word “Chinese” flashed into Mitya’s mind, “and behind the screen is Grushenka,” thought Mitya. He began watching Fyodor Pavlovitch, who was wearing a new striped-silk dressing-gown that Mitya had never seen, with a silk cord and tassels round the waist. A clean, dandified shirt of fine linen with gold studs peeped out under the collar of the dressing-gown. On his head Fyodor Pavlovitch had the same red bandage that Alyosha had seen.
“He’s dressed himself up,” thought Mitya.

His father was standing near the window, apparently lost in thought. Suddenly he jerked up his head and listened for a moment. Hearing nothing, he went up to the table, poured half a glass of brandy from a decanter and drank it off. Then he heaved a deep sigh and stood still again for a moment. He walked casually over to the looking-glass on the wall, lifted the red bandage on his forehead a little with his right hand, and began examining his bruises and scars, which had not yet gone away.
“He’s alone,” thought Mitya, “most likely he’s alone.”
Fyodor Pavlovitch moved away from the looking-glass, turned suddenly to the window and looked out. Mitya instantly slipped back into the shadow.

“She may be there behind the screen. Perhaps she’s asleep by now,” he thought, with a pang at his heart. Fyodor Pavlovitch moved away from the window. “He’s looking for her out of the window, so she’s not there. Why else would he stare out into the dark? He’s wild with impatience.” ... Mitya slipped back at once and went on gazing in at the window. The old man was sitting down at the table, apparently disappointed. At last he put his elbow on the table and laid his right cheek against his hand. Mitya watched him eagerly.
“He’s alone, he’s alone!” he repeated. “If she were here, his face would look different.”

Strange to say, a queer, senseless irritation rose in his heart that she was not here. “It’s not that she’s not here,” he explained to himself at once, “it’s that I can’t tell for certain whether she is or not.” Mitya remembered afterwards that his mind was exceptionally clear at that moment, that he took in everything down to the smallest detail and missed nothing. But a feeling of misery, the misery of uncertainty and indecision, grew in his heart with every instant. “Is she here or not?” The angry doubt filled his heart. Suddenly, making up his mind, he put out his hand and softly knocked on the window frame. He knocked the signal the old man had agreed on with Smerdyakov, twice slowly and then three times more quickly, the signal that meant “Grushenka is here!”
The old man started, jerked up his head, jumped up quickly and ran to the window. Mitya slipped away into the shadow. Fyodor Pavlovitch opened the window and thrust his whole head out.
“Grushenka, is it you? Is it you?” he said in a sort of trembling half-whisper. “Where are you, my angel, where are you?” He was terribly agitated and out of breath.
“He’s alone.” Mitya made up his mind.

“Where are you?” cried the old man again. He thrust his head out farther, out to the shoulders, gazing in all directions, right and left. “Come here, I’ve a little present for you. Come, I’ll show you....”
“He means the three thousand,” thought Mitya.
“But where are you? Are you at the door? I’ll open it right away.”

And the old man almost climbed out of the window, peering to the right, where there was a door into the garden, trying to see into the darkness. In another second he would certainly have run out to open the door, without waiting for Grushenka’s answer.

Mitya looked at him from the side without stirring. The old man’s profile, which he loathed so much, his hanging Adam’s apple, his hooked nose, his lips smiling in greedy expectation, were all brightly lit by the slanting lamplight falling from the room on the left. A horrible fury of hatred suddenly surged up in Mitya’s heart: “There he was, his rival, the man who had tormented him and ruined his life!” It was a rush of that sudden, furious, vengeful anger of which he had spoken to Alyosha, as though foreseeing it, four days ago in the arbor. Alyosha had asked him, “How can you say you’ll kill our father?” and he had answered, “I don’t know, I don’t know. Perhaps I shall not kill him, perhaps I shall. I’m afraid he’ll suddenly be so loathsome to me at that moment. I hate his double chin, his nose, his eyes, his shameless grin. I feel a personal repulsion. That’s what I’m afraid of, that’s what may be too much for me.” ... This personal repulsion was becoming unendurable. Mitya was beside himself. Suddenly he pulled the brass pestle out of his pocket.

“God was watching over me then,” Mitya himself said afterwards. At that very moment Grigory woke up on his sickbed. Earlier in the evening he had gone through the treatment that Smerdyakov had described to Ivan. He had rubbed himself all over with vodka mixed with a secret, very strong brew, and had drunk what was left of the mixture while his wife said a “certain prayer” over him. After that he had gone to bed. Marfa Ignatyevna had tasted the stuff too, and, being unused to strong drink, slept like the dead beside her husband.

But Grigory woke in the night, quite suddenly. After a moment’s thought, though he felt a sharp pain in his back at once, he sat up in bed. Then he thought again, got up and dressed hurriedly. Perhaps his conscience troubled him at the thought of sleeping while the house was unguarded “in such perilous times.” Smerdyakov, worn out by his fit, lay motionless in the next room. Marfa Ignatyevna did not stir. “The stuff’s been too much for the woman,” Grigory thought, glancing at her, and groaning he went out onto the steps. No doubt he only meant to look out from the steps, for he could hardly walk. The pain in his back and his right leg was intolerable. But he suddenly remembered that he had not locked the little gate into the garden that evening. He was the most punctual and exact of men, a man who kept to an unchanging routine and to habits that lasted for years. Limping and writhing with pain, he went down the steps and toward the garden. Yes, the gate stood wide open. Mechanically he stepped into the garden. Perhaps he imagined something, perhaps he caught some sound. Glancing to the left, he saw his master’s window open. No one was looking out of it just then.

“Why is it open? It’s not summer now,” thought Grigory. And at that very instant he caught a glimpse of something extraordinary in the garden ahead of him. Forty paces in front of him a man seemed to be running in the dark. Some sort of shadow was moving very fast.

“Good Lord!” cried Grigory, beside himself, and forgetting the pain in his back, he hurried to cut off the running figure. He took a short cut. Evidently he knew the garden better. The fleeing figure made for the bath-house, ran behind it and rushed to the garden fence. Grigory followed, never losing sight of him, and ran, forgetting everything. He reached the fence at the very moment the man was climbing over it. Grigory cried out, beside himself, pounced on him, and clutched his leg in both hands.
Yes, his foreboding had not deceived him. He recognized him. It was he, the “monster,” the “parricide.”
“Parricide!” the old man shouted so that the whole neighborhood could hear. But he had no time to shout more. He fell at once, as though struck by lightning.

Mitya jumped back into the garden and bent over the fallen man. In Mitya’s hand was a brass pestle, and he flung it mechanically into the grass. The pestle landed two paces from Grigory, not in the grass but on the path, in a very conspicuous place. For some seconds he examined the figure lying before him. The old man’s head was covered with blood. Mitya put out his hand and began feeling it. He remembered clearly afterwards that he had been desperately anxious to make sure whether he had broken the old man’s skull or only stunned him with the pestle. But the blood was flowing horribly, and in a moment Mitya’s fingers were drenched in the hot stream. He remembered taking out of his pocket the clean white handkerchief he had provided for his visit to Madame Hohlakov, and putting it to the old man’s head, senselessly trying to wipe the blood from his face and temples. But the handkerchief was instantly soaked with blood.

“Good heavens! What am I doing this for?” thought Mitya, suddenly pulling himself together. “If I’ve broken his skull, how can I find out now? And what difference does it make now?” he added, hopelessly. “If I’ve killed him, I’ve killed him.... You’ve come to grief, old man, so there you must lie!” he said aloud. And suddenly turning to the fence, he vaulted over it into the lane and started running—he held the blood-soaked handkerchief crushed up in his right fist, and as he ran he thrust it into the back pocket of his coat. He ran headlong. The few passers-by who met him in the dark streets remembered afterwards that they had met a man running that night. He flew back again to the widow Morozov’s house.

Right after he had left it that evening, Fenya had rushed to the head porter, Nazar Ivanovitch, and begged him, for Christ’s sake, “not to let the captain in again today or tomorrow.” Nazar Ivanovitch promised. But then he went upstairs to his mistress, who had suddenly sent for him. On the way up he met his nephew, a boy of twenty who had recently come from the country, and told him to take his place, but forgot to mention “the captain.” Mitya ran up to the gate and knocked. The lad recognized him at once, for Mitya had tipped him more than once. He opened the gate immediately and let him in, and hastened to tell him, with a good-humored smile, that “Agrafena Alexandrovna is not at home now, you know.”
“Where is she then, Prohor?” asked Mitya, stopping short.
“She set off this evening, some two hours ago, with Timofey, for Mokroe.”
“What for?” cried Mitya.
“That I can’t say. To see some officer. Someone invited her, and horses were sent to fetch her.”
Mitya left him and ran like a madman to Fenya.
